Lacquer is a liquid substance that you apply onto a surface — like wood, metal, or even fingernails — and once it dries, it forms a hard, smooth, glossy shell on top of that surface. Think of it as a transparent or lightly coloured "skin" that seals and protects whatever is underneath. It is shinier and harder than most paints, and its finish looks almost glass-like.
What it actually does to a surface

When you coat something with lacquer and let it dry, the result is a surface that:

  • Looks polished and glossy — it reflects light beautifully
  • Feels smooth and hard — almost like a thin sheet of plastic or glass sitting on top of the object
  • Is protected — from moisture, dust, minor scratches, and the effects of air

This is why lacquer is so commonly used on wooden furniture, musical instruments (especially guitars, where you can see that deep, glassy shine), and decorative objects. It doesn't just beautify — it also preserves.
Two kinds of lacquer you should know
There are two broad types, and they're quite different in origin:

This comes from the sap of a lacquer tree, found naturally in East Asia (China, Japan, Korea). When this sap is harvested and applied to a surface in thin layers, it hardens into an incredibly durable and beautiful finish. This natural lacquer has been used for thousands of years to make bowls, boxes, trays, and furniture — which is why you'll hear the word "lacquerware" used for these traditional East Asian objects. The deep, rich red-and-black items you often see in Chinese or Japanese art? Those are typically made using this natural lacquer.

This is what most people encounter in everyday life today. It's made from manufactured chemicals — like nitrocellulose or acrylic resins — dissolved in a solvent. When you spray or brush it onto a surface, the solvent evaporates quickly and leaves behind that hard, glossy coating. This type of lacquer is used widely in furniture manufacturing, car interiors, flooring, and industrial products.
How lacquer differs from paint and varnish

These three are often confused, so it helps to understand the difference:

  • Paint adds colour to a surface and makes it opaque (you can't see through it). Lacquer is usually clear or only lightly tinted — it lets the material underneath show through.
  • Varnish is also a clear protective coating, but it tends to be thicker, slower-drying, and gives a slightly softer finish than lacquer. Lacquer dries very fast, and its finish is notably harder and glossier.
  • One key technical trait of lacquer: it dries primarily by solvent evaporation, not by a chemical reaction with air. This means if you apply a fresh coat of lacquer over a dried one, they actually re-dissolve slightly into each other and bond together seamlessly — which makes touch-ups and repairs much easier than with varnish or paint.

You'll encounter "lacquer" used in these common contexts:

  • Nail lacquer — another word for nail polish; it's the same idea: a fast-drying glossy coating that hardens on your nails
  • Hair lacquer — a stiff hairspray that holds your hair in place by coating the strands with a light, hardening film (more commonly called "hair lacquer" in British English)
  • Lacquer finish — describes the surface treatment on a piece of furniture or a musical instrument
  • Lacquerware — objects (usually decorative or functional items like bowls, trays, and boxes) that have been coated with layers of lacquer, especially in the traditional East Asian style

Lacquer is a fast-drying liquid coating — either natural (from tree sap) or synthetic (from chemicals) — that, once applied to a surface and dried, forms a hard, smooth, and typically shiny protective layer over that surface.
